title: From Microbiome Associations to Deployable Precision Probiotics in Animals: A Critical Narrative Review and Proposed Causal Evidence Framework for Next-Generation Probiotic Development.
journal: Animals : an open access journal from MDPI
abstract: Next-generation probiotics (NGPs) are promoted as precision tools for animal health, yet the term is often applied to uncommon taxa before causality, safety and target-species efficacy are established. This critical narrative review reframes animal NGPs as a development pathway rather than a taxonomic category. A structured PubMed search was last run on 14 September 2026 with a publication date cutoff of 1 September 2026 and was supplemented by citation tracing and targeted searches of authoritative sources. From the screened literature, 45 representative and conceptually informative sources were purposively selected for the final narrative synthesis; the review was not intended to provide systematic or exhaustive coverage. The detailed synthesis focused on terrestrial farm and companion animals, whereas equine, rabbit and aquaculture studies were treated as boundary evidence. We evaluate how strain-resolved metagenomics, culturomics, metatranscriptomics, metaproteomics, metabolomics, host transcriptomics, machine learning, metabolic modeling and perturbation systems can move discovery beyond association. Studies across animal sectors show many biomarkers but limited causal validation, strain tracking, formulation data, multisite trials and ecological safety assessment. We propose an author-developed conceptual framework comprising a cumulative evidence ladder, from reproducible associations to field-ready deployment, and the ANIMAL-NGP reporting checklist (Animal endotype, Native ecological fit, Identity and genomic safety, Mechanism, Administration and manufacturing, and Longitudinal validation). These tools are intended to align claims with evidence and require prospective application and external validation. Multi-omics should therefore function as an evidence-navigation system, not as a substitute for causality.

title: Ovulation Timing After Recombinant Human Chorionic Gonadotropin, Gonadorelin, or Buserelin Under Estrus-Triggered and Fixed-Time Treatment Protocols for Artificial Insemination in Sows.
journal: Animals : an open access journal from MDPI
abstract: Precise coordination between ovulation and insemination is essential for optimizing fixed-time artificial insemination (FTAI) in sows. This study compared ovulation timing and reproductive outcomes after treatment with recombinant human chorionic gonadotropin (rhCG), gonadorelin, or buserelin under estrus-triggered and fixed-time treatment protocols. A total of 285 sows received equine chorionic gonadotropin 24 h after weaning. In Trial 1, the ovulation-inducing treatments were administered at estrus onset, whereas in Trial 2 they were administered 72 h after equine chorionic gonadotropin. Ovulation was monitored by transabdominal ultrasonography. In Trial 1, no significant differences in ovulation timing or reproductive performance were detected among treatments. In Trial 2, no significant differences were detected among treatments in the proportion of sows with ovulation detected within 72 h (p = 0.847), the overall time-to-event distributions (log-rank p = 0.790), or the variability in detected ovulation timing (Brown-Forsythe p = 0.884). Among rhCG-treated sows in which ovulation was detected, all observed ovulations occurred between 37 and 54 h after treatment. No statistically significant differences in reproductive outcomes were detected among treatments. These findings provide new information on the temporal ovulatory response to rhCG under fixed-time treatment and may inform further refinement of insemination timing in sow FTAI protocols.

title: Apparent Ca Test Positivity and Crossmatch Reactivity in Donkeys from Italy: Intraspecies and Horse-Donkey Compatibility.
journal: Animals : an open access journal from MDPI
abstract: Blood group distribution and serological compatibility are poorly characterized in donkeys. We estimated the apparent Ca positive-test frequency in 84 domestic donkeys and assessed donkey-donkey and horse-donkey crossmatch reactivity. Ca typing was performed using a commercial equine immunochromatographic assay. For donkey-donkey crossmatching, one major and one minor crossmatch were analyzed for each of the 77 Ca-concordant and 34 Ca-discordant pairs. Fifty-six of eighty-four donkeys yielded a positive result with the equine Ca assay (66.7%; 95% CI, 56.1-75.8%). Major combined macroscopic/microscopic reactivity occurred in 18/77 Ca-concordant and 11/34 Ca-discordant pairs, whereas minor combined reactivity occurred in 21/77 and 8/34 pairs, respectively. In crossed random-effects logistic models, the adjusted odds ratios for Ca-discordant versus Ca-concordant pairs were 1.56 (95% CI, 0.64-3.82) for major combined reactivity, 0.82 (95% CI, 0.32-2.10) for minor combined reactivity, and 1.57 (95% CI, 0.41-5.94) for major macroscopic reactivity; the minor macroscopic model was not estimable. Horse-donkey reactions were frequent and direction-dependent. When donkey plasma was tested against horse RBCs, combined reactivity occurred in 80/80 tests in the horse-donor/donkey-recipient dataset and in 76/76 tests in the reciprocal dataset, with macroscopic reactivity in 77/80 (96.3%) and 74/76 (97.4%), respectively. In the reciprocal horse-plasma/donkey-RBC direction, combined reactivity occurred in 53/80 (66.3%) and 51/76 (67.1%) tests, with macroscopic reactivity in 32/80 (40.0%) and 32/76 (42.1%), respectively. Ca concordance was not significantly associated with crossmatch reactivity in the present dataset, and Ca status alone did not account for the observed crossmatch-reactivity pattern.

title: Cranial Shape Variation in Adult Kyrgyz Horses: Associations with Size and Sex.
journal: Animals : an open access journal from MDPI
abstract: Cranial diversity within indigenous horse populations remains incompletely characterized. Cranial shape variation and its associations with skull size and sex were investigated in 37 adult Kyrgyz horses aged 4-5 years (18 females and 19 males). Three-dimensional configurations of 25 cranial landmarks were evaluated using Procrustes alignment, principal component analysis, and permutation-based multivariate models. Skull size was quantified using centroid size calculated from the landmark configurations. The first two principal components represented 29.41% of shape variance, with changes distributed across multiple cranial regions and substantial overlap between sexes. A 5.42% greater mean centroid size was observed in males (p 0.05). Small, localized differences were observed between adjusted mean configurations. Cranial variation was therefore characterized by changes across several anatomical regions, a modest association with size, and limited evidence for additional sexual shape differentiation after size adjustment.

title: Teaching Direction Control in Horse Riding: A Pre-Post Intervention Proof-of-Concept Study Using Multi-Modal Motor Learning Techniques.
journal: Animals : an open access journal from MDPI
abstract: Many riders experience persistent communication problems with their horses, particularly in controlling speed and direction, despite extensive training. This proof-of-concept study employed a pre-test-post-test intervention design to examine the effectiveness of the Four-Step Riding Programme (FSRP) in developing clear rider-horse body language for direction control. Multi-modal motor learning techniques (MMLTs) were applied to five rider-horse dyads during four one-hour lessons to teach coordinated movement patterns necessary for directional accuracy. Rider-horse communication was evaluated before and after the intervention using video recordings of 13 riding exercises. Three independent assessors rated the performances on a 5-point Likert scale, and riders provided self-assessments on the same scale. Horse stride parameters, reflecting shoulder control, were visualised with the Alogo™ Move Pro electronic sensor. Significant improvements were observed between pre- and post-intervention scores across all assessors and participants (p < 0.05). These preliminary findings suggest that the FSRP holds promise for facilitating the acquisition of rider-horse body language necessary for precise direction control.

title: The Western Ecotype of the Kazakh Horse: Current Status and Genomic Characterisation.
abstract: Background/Objectives: The Kazakh horse comprises several locally adapted types and ecotypes of the Eurasian Steppe. The Adai is its western ecotype, kept year-round on desert pasture in Mangystau, Western Kazakhstan, and recognised as a separate breed in 2024 without genetic evaluation. We asked whether that label corresponds to a genetic unit and whether the population has remained closed. Methods: We genotyped 533 horses recorded as Adai, 500 traced to five farms in Mangystau, against 988 reference horses of 45 breeds on 36,193 shared autosomal SNPs. Structure was assessed by principal component analysis, pairwise FST with block-jackknife intervals, neighbour-joining trees and cross-validated individual assignment; introgression per animal by an f4 statistic against an empirical null of 223 reference-steppe horses, with the ancestry scale calibrated on 1800 simulated crosses built from real genotypes; and eight body measurements were modelled within farms. Results: The Adai was not separable from the Central Asian steppe complex as a population: pairwise FST was 0.004-0.008 against Tuva, Yili, Sanhe and Mongolian horses, and two Adai farms differed from each other as much as an Adai farm differed from a reference-steppe breed. Individual assignment was nonetheless accurate against those breeds (86-100% pairwise), but the same classifier separated two herds of Adai at 69-85%, so assignment accuracy on thousands of markers tracks marker number rather than breed identity. Against the empirical null, 15.6% of Adai exceeded the 95th percentile and twelve exceeded the maximum. The estimator carries a floor of 3.7 percentage points on an unadmixed Adai; on the calibrated scale, 9.6% of animals reached the ancestry expected from one Thoroughbred great-grandparent and 4.2% that expected from one grandparent (15.8% and 4.6% uncalibrated). Introgression was concentrated: one farm carried 42% of its horses at a great-grandparent equivalent or more against 0-9% at the other four, a difference that survived every analysis accounting for family structure. Ancestry showed no within-farm association with any of eight body measurements, with or without age in the model. Conclusions: The Adai is not a differentiated population but part of a continuous steppe complex, and carries undocumented ancestry of Thoroughbred affinity concentrated in particular holdings. As managed, it cannot be certified from a document or a phenotype. Genomic verification at registration is a plausible instrument, but the marker panel it would require was not developed or validated here.

title: Epidemiology of animal bites and post-exposure vaccination coverage in Davao City, Philippines: A five-year retrospective cohort study, 2019-2023.
abstract: Rabies remains a major public health threat in the Philippines, particularly in urban areas such as Davao City, where frequent animal bites from domestic reservoirs increase the transmission risk at the human-animal-environment interface. Detailed epidemiological data on animal bites and post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) coverage are limited. This One Health-framed retrospective cohort study describes trends in bite incidents, assesses PEP coverage, and identifies gaps in rabies prevention efforts from 2019 to 2023. Surveillance data from the Davao City Animal Bite Treatment Centers captured 98,442 cases. Dogs caused 63.5% of bites, with a significant upward trend (p = 0.027; τ = 1.0, 95% CI 0.200-1.800); cat bites (36.4%) rose sharply, indicating an emerging reservoir challenge. Children ≤15 years of age showed a significant increase (p = 0.027). The 3rd congressional district had the most pronounced rise across demographics and exposure categories. Tissue culture vaccine coverage remained at 100%, equine rabies immunoglobulin rose from 18.5% to 85.9%, whereas human rabies immunoglobulin remained low post-COVID. Despite universal TCV access, immunoglobulin gaps limit its control. Rising cat bites and severe exposures demand integrated One Health strategies, enhanced surveillance, animal vaccination, and supply chain strengthening, to achieve zero human rabies deaths by 2030.

title: Catastrophic distal sesamoidean ligament rupture in 72 racehorses in California.
journal: Journal of veterinary diagnostic investigation : official publication of the American Association of Veterinary Laboratory Diagnosticians, Inc
abstract: Rupture of major distal sesamoidean ligaments (DSLs) in racehorses results in suspensory apparatus failure. Our objective was to describe postmortem findings and exercise histories for Thoroughbred (TB) and Quarter Horse racehorses that had DSL rupture as the sole cause of catastrophic musculoskeletal and suspensory apparatus failure. We described horse signalment, activity at the time of injury, and postmortem findings and compared the exercise histories with those of event-matched control horses. In 72 racehorses, predominantly ≥4-y-old, catastrophic rupture of forelimb DSLs (41 left, 29 right, 2 bilateral) occurred while racing (61), training (9), or during non-exercise activity (2). DSL rupture occurred in isolation in 27 horses; the remaining 45 horses also had disruption of other ligaments and tendons secondary to associated fetlock or pastern disarticulation. Rupture of the DSLs involved the straight (69), oblique (68 medial, 69 lateral), cruciate (49), and short (49) DSLs. Complete rupture of the straight, oblique, cruciate, and short DSLs occurred more frequently (p < 0.05) in the proximal third of the pastern region (49 horses) than complete rupture of the straight and oblique DSLs in the distal third of the pastern region (23 horses). Two horses had chronic desmopathy in the proximal third of the oblique DSL. Proximal ruptures occurred more frequently in the left forelimb (p = 0.005). TB horses with DSL rupture had longer careers, more time in layup, and less high-speed activity in the year before injury than unaffected control horses. Complete rupture of the DSLs had a very low prevalence (1.4%) among catastrophic musculoskeletal injuries.

title: Thirteen years of environmental surveillance of ESKAPE organisms and Escherichia coli in an equine hospital: Informing infection control.
abstract: Bacteria from the ESKAPE group (i.e., Enterococcus faecium, Staphylococcus aureus, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Acinetobacter baumannii, Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Enterobacter species) and Escherichia coli are frequently multidrug-resistant and can be associated with healthcare-associated infections, an increasing concern for veterinary settings. To determine the environmental prevalence of ESKAPE and E. coli on surfaces which can act as reservoirs of infection in clinical areas in equine hospitals. Observational study. Routine environmental sampling was performed in one busy equine hospital with Swiffer® wipes to screen surfaces from high-risk areas (e.g., surgical theatres, intensive care unit [ICU], isolation unit), equipment (e.g., endotracheal tubes) and high-touch areas (e.g., keyboards) following selective species-specific protocols for each target organism. Monitoring hand-hygiene of hospital staff and students was by hand-plate sampling. After a pilot phase E. faecium was excluded from routine screening. Nine hundred and ninety-five environmental and hand-plate samples were collected from April 2010 to February 2023. The overall E. coli-SKAPE (E. coli, methicillin-resistant S. aureus [MRSA], K. pneumoniae, A. baumannii, P. aeruginosa and Enterobacter spp.) prevalence was 37.9%, where E. coli was the most (and K. pneumoniae the least) common target organism identified (18.0% and 1.7% respectively). E. coli was most prevalent in general stables and yards (37.7%) and offices (25.7%). Enterobacter spp. was the main organism in the environmental samples from ICU (24.2%) and isolation unit (22.9%, along with E. coli). Concerningly, hand-plate sampling showed that MRSA was the most common organism detected on hands (8.4%), followed by A. baumannii (5.2%) and E. cloacae (3.9%); however, E. coli, P. aeruginosa and K. pneumoniae were not found in these samples. Inconsistent sampling limited longitudinal analysis. We generated baseline environmental contamination data and demonstrated high E. coli-SKAPE hospital surface and hand contamination, informing infection control to prevent environment-to-patient cross-transmission.

title: Uncovering cardiac molecular remodelling in racing Thoroughbreds with paroxysmal atrial fibrillation.
abstract: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most common arrhythmia in both humans and horses, with a comparable prevalence of ~2%. In horses, AF is a major cause of poor athletic performance and linked to sudden cardiac death, yet its underlying molecular mechanisms remain poorly understood. To investigate transcriptomic remodelling associated with spontaneous paroxysmal AF (PAF). Case-control study. We performed RNA sequencing on left atrial (LA) tissue from three Thoroughbred racehorses with PAF and four matched controls. All horses were euthanised due to musculoskeletal reasons. Cell type deconvolution was performed with BayesPrism. The differential expression analysis was performed with EdgeR. Alternative splicing analysis was performed with SUPPA2. Cell-type deconvolution revealed a modest, non-significant shift towards increased fibroblast and immune cell proportions in PAF, but not enough to account for widespread transcriptional changes. 1400 of the 12,012 included genes were considered significantly differentially expressed (Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted p-value <0.05). These genes included ion channels, calcium-handling proteins, and conduction-related genes. In addition, several genes directly involved in cardiac muscle contraction and mitochondrial energy metabolism were differentially expressed. Alternative splicing analysis revealed over 20 significantly altered events, including skipped exons in genes with potential relevance to cardiac function and remodelling. The number of biological replicates was modest. Overall, despite no major changes in cell composition, the findings highlight intrinsic structural and molecular changes in the LA of PAF-affected horses. This study provides the first transcriptomic and splicing analysis of atrial tissue in racehorses with PAF, revealing molecular remodelling consistent with mechanisms of arrhythmia maintenance and suggesting potential targets for further functional investigation.

title: Harnessing CSC recruitment: photo-triggered "self-exploding" macrophages for targeted metastasis inhibition.
abstract: Cancer metastasis is a serious threat to human health. Cancer stem cells (CSC) are closely related to tumor metastasis, but it is difficult to achieve accurate drug delivery and effective inhibition of CSC due to the complex tumor microenvironment. Herein, we report a living cell delivery system, C-H@M2, engineered by loading M2 macrophages with carrier-free Ce6/Honokiol self-assembled nanoparticles. This system is designed to harness the tumor's intrinsic recruitment mechanism for targeted anti-metastasis therapy. Acting as a "Trojan Horse", C-H@M2 exploits the active recruitment of M2 macrophages by CSC to achieve precise tumor homing. Upon laser irradiation, the macrophages undergo photo-triggered immunogenic lysis ("self-explosion"), leading to the burst release of therapeutic payloads and the induction of robust immunogenic cell death (ICD). HK as an inhibitor of Forkhead box M1 (FOXM1) inhibits CSC stemness and epithelial mesenchymal transition (EMT) in tumor tissues. In vivo experimental results demonstrate that C-H@M2 significantly inhibits tumor and lung metastasis through a triple-modal strategy: Self-explosion enhanced ICD effect, stemness and EMT inhibition, CSC killing by stemness inhibition and PDT. Our study provides a novel strategy for CSC targeted therapy and cancer metastasis inhibition.

title: Infection and abduction loss predict equine laryngoplasty failure.
abstract: Prosthetic laryngoplasty (PL) is the most common surgical treatment for recurrent laryngeal neuropathy (RLN) in horses. Post-operative complications may compromise outcomes, and the influence of breed and anaesthetic approach remains unclear. To evaluate factors associated with surgical outcome at 3 months following PL, focusing on post-operative complications, anaesthetic modality and breed (particularly Iberian baroque breeds). Multicentre retrospective cohort study. Medical records from 181 horses across 7 equine hospitals using the same standardised surgical technique were reviewed. Variables including breed, anaesthesia type, ventriculocordectomy (VeC) method and post-operative complications were analysed using χ2 or Fisher's exact tests and Spearman correlation. Two binomial generalised linear mixed models, with surgeon as a random effect, evaluated pre/intra-operative predictors and post-operative prognostic factors. Level of significance p < 0.05. Surgical success was defined as the absence of respiratory noise and exercise intolerance at 3 months. Surgical success was achieved in 79.1% of cases. Complications occurred in 33.7% of horses and were negatively associated with treatment success (odds ratio [OR] 0.003; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.000-0.052; p < 0.001). Major loss of arytenoid abduction (18.2%) and surgical site infection (SSI; 6.6%) were the only variables independently associated with reduced odds of treatment success in the post-operative model (OR 0.011; 95% CI 0.001-0.178; p = 0.001 and OR 0.046; 95% CI 0.004-0.559; p = 0.016, respectively). Breed was not associated with surgical outcome. The retrospective multicentre design may introduce selection bias, variability in clinical practice and heterogeneous follow-up. Major loss of arytenoid abduction and SSI were the strongest predictors of failure, highlighting the importance of meticulous technique, preservation of arytenoid abduction and rigorous infection control to optimise outcomes after PL.

title: The genome sequence of horse-radish, Armoracia rusticana G.Gaertn., B.Mey. & Scherb. (Brassicales: Brassicaceae).
abstract: We present a genome assembly of Armoracia rusticana (horse-radish; Streptophyta; Magnoliopsida; Brassicales; Brassicaceae). The assembly consists of two haplotypes with total lengths of 605.90 megabases and 589.75 megabases. The haplotype 1 assembly and the haplotype 2 assembly each contain 16 chromosomal pseudomolecules; these account for 99.56% and 99.22% of their respective sequences. The mitochondrial genome assembly has a length of 316.39 kilobases and the plastid genome assemblies have lengths of 156.67 and 155.14 kilobases. Gene annotation of the haplotype 1 assembly by Ensembl identified 40,675 protein-coding genes. This assembly was generated as part of the Darwin Tree of Life project, which produces reference genomes for eukaryotic species found in Britain and Ireland.

title: Effects of acute dopamine infusion on metabolic and endocrine responses in horses with different endocrine phenotypes: an exploratory fixed-sequence study.
abstract: Dopamine modulates insulin secretion and sensitivity in other species, but its peripheral metabolic effects in horses remain unclear. We evaluated whether continuous dopamine hydrochloride (DA HCl) infusion alters oral carbohydrate-stimulated insulin responses or peripheral insulin sensitivity in horses with different metabolic classifications. Seven horses completed oral sugar tests (OST) and hyperinsulinemic-euglycemic clamps (EHC) under control conditions and during DA HCl infusion (2.5 µg/kg/min), with each horse serving as its own control. Horses were classified separately as normoinsulinemic (NI; n = 4) or hyperinsulinemic (HI; n = 3) based on OST responses and as insulin-sensitive (IS; n = 3) or insulin-resistant (IR; n = 4) using a study-specific cutoff derived from control EHC glucose infusion rate (GIR). During the OST, DA HCl did not significantly alter glucose or insulin profiles or their areas under the curve. During the EHC, exploratory insulin-sensitivity classification × treatment interactions were detected for GIR (P < 0.01) and insulin sensitivity index (M/I; P = 0.047); however, within-group treatment effects were not statistically significant. Acute DA HCl infusion markedly suppressed circulating prolactin but did not significantly alter oral carbohydrate-stimulated insulin responses. Exploratory EHC findings suggest that responses to acute DA HCl infusion may differ according to insulin-sensitivity classification. Given the small sample size, study-specific classification, fixed treatment sequence, and multiple comparisons, these findings require confirmation in a larger, randomized study.

title: Microscopic and Biological Characterization of Cryopreserved Equine Umbilical Tissue Allograft.
abstract: Equicenta®CTM is a cryopreserved micronized equine umbilical-derived tissue allograft (eUTA) that is minimally processed and contains an abundance of fetal proteins in a connective tissue matrix. This study aimed to characterize this eUTA's microscopic structure, biodegradation, and potential to release biologically relevant proteins from a tissue scaffold reservoir, including cytokines, growth factors, and extracellular vesicles (EVs). Microscopic evaluation of eUTA was performed using stereoscopic culture and pelleted smears. In vitro enzymatic digestion with collagenase or trypsin (positive control) in tissue culture suspensions was used to assess morphological changes. A 24-hour digestion study quantified the total protein, collagen type 1 alpha chain 1 (Col1A1), and tissue inhibitor of metalloproteinase-2 (TIMP-2). Anabolic, anti-inflammatory, and anti-catabolic biomediators were measured using multiplex ELISA before and after detergent extraction. EVs were evaluated by nanoparticle tracking analysis and tetraspanin detection. Microscopy revealed free-floating microparticle aggregates and fibrillar net-like extracellular matrix scaffolds in a proteinaceous ground substance. Collagenase caused gradual matrix breakdown, whereas trypsin resulted in rapid, complete degradation. The eUTA contained multiple cytokines and growth factors; selected anabolic and anti-catabolic proteins increased after scaffold digestion or extraction, including insulin-like growth factor (IGF-1), alpha-2 macroglobulin (A2M), and TIMP-2. (Col1A1) was released continuously over 24 hours during collagenase digestion. EV analysis confirmed abundant particles expressing CD9, CD63, and CD81. Microscopic evaluation of eUTA revealed an intricate filamentous microparticle matrix capable of serving as a scaffold for endogenous tissue repair in orthopedic injuries. This matrix can be degraded by naturally occurring proteolytic collagenases, thereby releasing matrix proteins and bioactive factors over time, which may support healing.

title: Generation of polycistronic lentivirus-induced pluripotent stem cells from Mongolian horse embryonic fibroblasts.
abstract: Pluripotent stem cells are considered highly promising in both human and veterinary medicine. In this study, Mongolian horse embryonic fibroblasts were successfully reprogrammed into equine-induced pluripotent stem cells using a polycistronic lentiviral vector encoding human OCT4, SOX2, c-MYC, and KLF4. The resulting cells exhibited morphological similarities to previously reported iPSCs from other species and demonstrated long-term stable proliferation in vitro. Quantitative PCR analysis revealed that these cells expressed endogenous OCT4 and SOX2 while simultaneously expressing pluripotency genes NANOG, REX1, LIN28A, FGF5, ESRRB, and OTX2. The cell surface markers SSEA1 and SSEA4 were detected as positive. Under appropriate culture conditions, these equine iPSCs efficiently formed embryoid bodies and further differentiated into cells expressing markers for ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm. Factor depletion experiments demonstrated that equine iPSCs severely lost their original clonal morphology in the absence of bFGF, whereas this phenomenon does not occur upon depletion of LIF. These findings indicate that, similar to human iPSCs, bFGF supports the maintenance of the undifferentiated state of equine iPSCs. The equine iPSC lines established in this study provide tools for elucidating early developmental mechanisms.

title: Bayesian estimation of genetic parameters and comparison of statistical models for race performance traits in the Turkmen horse.
journal: Animal : an international journal of animal bioscience
abstract: Racing performance is an important component of genetic evaluation and breeding decisions in racehorses, but it is a complex trait influenced by genetic and multiple non-genetic factors, including race conditions, management, handicap, and jockey effects. Different specifications of these effects may produce different estimates of genetic parameters and breeding values, highlighting the need to compare alternative model structures. This study aimed to estimate genetic parameters, compare alternative statistical models, and evaluate their suitability for genetic evaluation of racing performance traits in the Turkmen horses bred in Iran. Data comprised 10 830 official race records from 1 667 horses, including 899 stallions and 768 mares, collected from 2003 to 2023. Three racing performance traits were evaluated using eight hierarchical models that differed in their random-effect structures. Model 8 (M8) was selected as the best-supported model for all three race performance traits, including race completion time (RCT), rank at the end of competition (REC), and average speed (AS). Heritability estimates were 0.006 ± 0.001 for RCT, 0.06 ± 0.01 for REC, and 0.004 ± 0.001 for AS. Prediction bias ranged from 0.12 to 0.20, and prediction accuracy ranged from 0.60 to 0.78. The low heritability estimates indicate that additive genetic variance accounted for a relatively small proportion of phenotypic variation in this population under the models considered. Although the parameter estimates and model rankings are population-specific, the findings illustrate a broader methodological consideration for genetic evaluation of racing performance: model specification should account for relevant race-level and jockey-related effects when these factors contribute substantially to observed performance. This consideration may inform genetic evaluation strategies in other racing horse populations with similarly complex performance environments.

title: Sarcocystis sp. infection associated to encephalomyelitis and myositis in a Brazilian dog.
abstract: Sarcocystis sp.-induced disease is known especially in horses, in which S. neurona is the primary causative agent of Equine Protozoal Myeloencephalitis in the Americas. While horses are aberrant hosts, the range of susceptible species includes marine mammals, raccoons, and cats. Reports of clinical disease in dogs are rare, remaining unreported in South America. This study describes the clinical, pathological, and immunohistochemical findings of a naturally occurring, fatal case of meningoencephalomyelitis and myositis caused by Sarcocystis sp. in a dog in Brazil. A 5-year-old mixed-breed bitch presented with acute non-ambulatory tetraparesis, generalized muscle atrophy, and blindness. Despite supportive therapy, the patient deteriorated and was euthanized. Gross findings included enlarged lymph nodes, moderate splenomegaly and hepatomegaly, with multifocal mild fibrin deposition on the liver capsule, accompanied by multifocal mild hemorrhages in the pancreas. Histopathology demonstrated severe, multifocal necrotizing meningoencephalomyelitis, myositis, splenitis, lymphadenitis and interstitial pneumonia, associated with intralesional protozoal schizonts. Immunohistochemistry supported immunolabelling consistent with Sarcocystis sp. while excluding Toxoplasma gondii and Neospora caninum. To the authors' knowledge, this represents the first report of clinical canine sarcocystosis with this severity in South America supported by histopathological and immunohistochemical findings. These findings support that Sarcocystis sp. should be considered a differential diagnosis for canine progressive neurological disease, highlighting the potential role of wildlife reservoirs in the disease's epidemiology.

title: Multimodal Analysis of Child-Horse Therapeutic Interactions Using Vision-Language Models in an Australian Aboriginal Equine-Assisted Learning Program for Social and Emotional Well-Being: Development and Evaluation Study.
abstract: The human-horse bond has played a role in human development throughout history and has more recently been applied to mental health promotion through equine-assisted learning (EAL) programs. In EAL settings, therapeutic documentation and assessment commonly rely on practitioner observations documented through behavioral checklists, structured interviews, and progress notes, which can pose challenges due to time demands, subjectivity, and inconsistent standardization across practitioners and contexts. This study aimed to address these challenges in the context of mental health promotion programs. This study developed an AI-powered digital health framework based on vision-language models (VLMs) to analyze child-horse therapeutic interactions in EAL settings. The framework was developed in collaboration with the Yawardani Jan-ga EAL program, which supports the social and emotional well-being of Aboriginal youth in the Kimberley region of Western Australia. The proposed framework comprises three core components: (1) an activity classification module using a VLM with few-shot learning based on Sigmoid Loss for Language-Image Pre-training 2 (SigLIP2) to identify 9 therapeutic activities; (2) a proxemics analysis module using a Qwen2.5-VL-7B VLM to classify physical contact between the child and horse; and (3) a body posture analysis module applying multimodal chain-of-thought prompting and self-consistency techniques to classify children's body posture into confidence-related states with interpretable reasoning. The framework was developed and evaluated using real-world images collected during therapeutic sessions with Aboriginal children participating in the Yawardani Jan-ga program. The activity classification module achieved an accuracy of 90.6%, with macroaveraged precision, recall, and F1-scores of 92.0%, 91.1%, and 91.1%, respectively, under the selected 2-shot configuration. The proxemics analysis module achieved an accuracy of 88.6%, with macroaveraged precision, recall, and F1-scores of 89.0%, 88.0%, and 88.5%, respectively, under the 1-shot configuration. For the body posture analysis module, system reliability was assessed using internal consistency metrics, achieving an average consistency of 0.916, an agreement rate of 0.705, a rationale coherence of 0.857, and a vote entropy of 0.174. Overall, the findings suggest that AI- and VLM-based approaches can provide complementary support for practitioner-led documentation and assessment of observable child-horse therapeutic interactions in EAL settings. These approaches may help reduce practitioner burden and strengthen the assessment of programs that promote children's social and emotional well-being.

title: The influence of a systemic non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug on growth factors and cytokines in equine plasma, solid platelet-rich fibrin (PRF), and liquid PRF.
abstract: Platelet-rich fibrin (PRF) is a second-generation platelet concentrate that contains growth factors and cytokines within a fibrin matrix, allowing prolonged release and supporting its use as a regenerative therapy for corneal wound healing. Horses with ulcerative keratitis are commonly treated with systemic NSAIDs; therefore, it is clinically important to determine whether prolonged flunixin meglumine alters the composition of PRF or plasma. To evaluate the effects of systemic NSAID administration on bio-analyte concentrations in equine plasma, solid PRF, and liquid PRF, and to compare these concentrations among blood products. Prospective, cross-sectional study. Horses were enrolled into two groups: horses treated with systemic full-dose flunixin meglumine (1.1 mg/kg BID) for three or more days (NSAID group) and horses without NSAID exposure for three or more months (control group). Plasma and PRF preparation followed standard protocols and concentrations for growth factors and cytokines were quantified using multiplex immunoassay or ELISA. Flunixin meglumine concentrations in plasma were measured via LC-MS/MS. Differences between treatment groups (NSAID vs. control) and between analyte concentrations were statistically compared across blood products; p < 0.05 was considered significant. NSAID group: n = 12 horses and control group: n = 12 horses. Solid PRF from the control group had significantly higher concentrations of TGF-β1, PDGF, and VEGF-A compared to the NSAID group. Analysis across the three blood products showed plasma had significantly higher concentrations of TGF-β1 and TGF-β2, whereas solid PRF had significantly higher concentrations of PDGF, IL-1β, IL-4, and TNF-α. Small sample size and incomplete characterisation of horses' metabolic and endocrine status. Systemic NSAID administration appears to reduce concentrations of key growth factors in solid PRF. Combined use of plasma and solid PRF may maximise delivery of evaluated growth factors and cytokines.

title: Colonic adenocarcinoma with osseous metaplasia and systemic metastasis in a horse.
journal: The Canadian veterinary journal = La revue veterinaire canadienne
abstract: A 12-year-old thoroughbred mare was presented with colic and diarrhea. Clinical examination revealed mild tachycardia with injected mucous membranes. Abdominal ultrasonography identified thickened colon walls, an irregular, mottled liver, and free fluid. The mare had elevated liver enzymes and electrolyte abnormalities that continued to worsen during hospitalization and included hypoalbuminemia. Despite intensive and varied medical treatments, the mare's condition deteriorated and she was humanely euthanized. Postmortem examination revealed a large adenocarcinoma with osseous metaplasia in the right dorsal colon and mesocolon with multifocal metastasis.

title: Influence of the anaesthetist´s perception on the evaluation of recovery quality in horses undergoing general anaesthesia.
abstract: In horses, anaesthetic recovery is evaluated using subjective scales. Previous studies examined the influence of scale type and evaluator-related factors but the impact of operator perception (unconscious bias) has received limited attention. To analyse the influence of operator perception on recovery scoring. Anaesthetic recoveries at an equine hospital (May 2019-May 2023) were assessed in real time (RT) by attending anaesthetists and retrospectively using video recordings (VR) by a single evaluator. Horses aged 1 - 21 years undergoing a single anesthetic procedure with complete video recordings were included. Recovery quality was scored using a simple scale (SS; 1 = excellent to 5 = dangerous) and a detailed scale (DS; 0 = very violent to 5 = no ataxia). RT and VR were compared using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test. A secondary analysis included only cases evaluated by the same anaesthetist in both conditions. Exploratory analyses assessed influences of time of day, procedure, anaesthesia duration, number of standing attempts and grouped recovery categories. Analyses were performed using SPSS (IBM) (p < 0.05). Of 262 recoveries, 154 met inclusion criteria. VR scores were significantly worse than RT assessment for both scales [SS: 2 (IQR: 1); DS: 4 (IQR: 1)], including same-evaluator cases [SS: 2 (IQR: 2); DS: 4 (IQR: 1)]. Discrepancies persisted across most subgroups but were not observed in unsatisfactory recoveries, or for DS scores during nighttime or horses presenting ≥3 standing attempts. Anaesthetists tend to assign more favourable scores when evaluating their own patients in RT, suggesting an optimism bias.

title: Applications of flow cytometry in equine medicine: current clinical and research perspectives.
abstract: Flow cytometry is a powerful analytical technique that enables rapid, quantitative, and multiparametric assessment of individual cells in suspension. Owing to its ability to evaluate cellular morphology, viability, and the expression of specific surface and intracellular markers, it has become an indispensable tool in biomedical research and clinical diagnostics. Over the past two decades, significant advances in cytometric technologies and the increasing availability of species-specific reagents have expanded the applicability of flow cytometry in equine medicine. This review highlights the predominantly research-based applications of flow cytometry in horses and their potential to address diagnostic gaps and complement conventional diagnostic methods. Particular attention is given to its principal applications in equine clinical immunology, including peripheral blood lymphocyte immunophenotyping; oncology, through the characterization of hematopoietic and lymphoid neoplasms; internal medicine, via cytometric evaluation of bronchoalveolar lavage fluid; and andrology, where flow cytometry serves as a valuable tool for the assessment of stallion semen quality. The article also highlights recent developments and discusses the growing role of flow cytometry as a diagnostic and research platform in contemporary equine medicine.

title: High proportion of horses in Germany positive for antibodies against Anoplocephalidae.
abstract: Tapeworms are often overlooked intestinal parasites in horses, although infections can potentially cause clinical disease. Antibody-detection-based diagnostic methods have significant advantages for estimating the proportion of horses positive for tapeworms, as some faecal routine examinations are often limited by low sensitivity. Data were obtained in the federal states Brandenburg, Bavaria, Lower Saxony, North Rhine-Westphalia, Saxony and Schleswig-Holstein. Coproscopy was performed using the Mini-FLOTAC technique (n = 970). Antibodies against the Anoplocephala perfoliata excretory-secretory 12-13 kDa antigen complex were measured using saliva- (n = 969) and plasma- (n = 957) based ELISAs (n = 923 paired samples). These data were combined with responses to a questionnaire to assess risk factors associated with tapeworm infection. Tapeworm eggs were found in 0.7% (n = 7) faecal samples. Saliva-based ELISA testing identified positive tapeworm results in 20.1% of horses, with 60.4% of yards having at least one positive horse, while in the plasma-based ELISA, 11.0% of horses and 47.4% of yards were positive. Risk factor analysis using multivariable generalised estimating equations for binomial data, based on saliva ELISA results, showed that geographical origin was a significant determinant of infection risk. Horses from Brandenburg had the highest odds of testing positive (odds ratio [OR] 18.7; proportion 42.1%), while horses from Lower Saxony, Saxony and North Rhine-Westphalia also showed significantly higher odds (OR 4.1-12.4; proportion 17.4-32.2%) compared with Schleswig-Holstein (4.0%). Bavaria was the only state that did not differ significantly from Schleswig-Holstein (OR 2.7; proportion 9.0%). Another important factor was age: horses under 1 year (OR 0.41) or older than 5 years (OR 0.43) had significantly lower odds (P < 0.001) compared to horses aged 1-5 years. Strongyle faecal egg counts increased the odds of individuals being Anoplocephala-positive, with odds increasing 1.07-fold with every increase in egg counts by 100 (P < 0.001). The ELISA results show that horses in Germany are more frequently positive for Anoplocephalidae than indicated by Mini-FLOTAC. Strong regional differences in tapeworm saliva test positivity and the relatively low number of horses treated against tapeworms emphasise the importance of applying tapeworm diagnostics in control programmes.

title: Seroprevalence of equine leptospirosis in Connecticut, US.
abstract: Leptospirosis is a geographically widespread neglected zoonotic disease caused by pathogenic spirochetes of the Leptospira genus. Horses can act as subclinical reservoir hosts, which are characterized as asymptomatic carriers that persistently excrete leptospires through their urine and transmit the disease. Horses play an important role in the lives of Connecticut (CT) residents in the form of leisure pursuits and related business activities. Nevertheless, there is a limited understanding of horse exposure to Leptospira in CT. This investigation sought to determine the prevalence of anti-Leptospira antibodies in horses in Connecticut, US. A total of 397 sera were tested by the microscopic agglutination test (MAT). The antigen panel included 40 strains representing 26 serogroups and four autochthonous isolates (not determined serogroup). The overall horse seropositivity (established as a titer ≥ 1:100) was 61.5% (244/397). The most detected serogroups were Djasiman, Grippotyphosa, Australis, Pomona, Icterohaemorrhagiae, and serovar Room22 strain GWTS1. Cross reaction for more than one serogroup was found in 80/244 (32.8%). As a limitation, the MAT does not differentiate between natural exposure and vaccination. However, Leptospira bacterin for horses includes only serogroup Pomona in the U.S. Therefore, after eliminating Pomona results to reduce potential vaccination bias, the seroprevalence was 204/397 (51.4%). Our results showed a high seroprevalence of leptospirosis in Connecticut and strong evidence that animals were potentially exposed to serogroups/serovars not included in commercial bacterins. Further studies to attempt isolation and genotyping of the pathogen from horses are necessary to better understand the role of horses in the epidemiology of leptospirosis. This information will support diagnostic strategies, vaccine recommendations, risk assessment, and public health actions that can reduce spillover transmission and the impact of this important zoonotic disease.

title: West Nile virus in Portugal: insights from equine serology.
abstract: West Nile virus (WNV) is a zoonotic mosquito-borne flavivirus belonging to the family Flaviviridae and the genus Orthoflavivirus. It is primarily transmitted by Culex spp. mosquitoes and maintained in an enzootic cycle involving avian hosts. Humans and horses are considered incidental or dead-end hosts, as they do not sustain onward transmission due to their low viremia levels, although infections may progress to severe neurological disease and death. In Portugal, WNV has circulated in horses almost annually since its first detection in 2004, suggesting endemic establishment. This study provides updated data on the geographical distribution and annual occurrence of WNV infection in clinically affected horses in mainland Portugal between 2022 and 2025, thereby contributing to a broader understanding of WNV dynamics in southern Europe. As viremia is typically low and short-lived in horses, diagnosis relies primarily on serological methods, particularly the detection of IgM antibodies. IgM analyses identified WNV-seropositive horses in all four years, with 3/9 cases (33.3%) testing positive in 2022, 15/30 (50.0%) in 2023, 32/52 (61.5%) in 2024, and 13/38 (34.2%) in 2025. No WNV RNA was detected in serum samples. Based on clinical signs together with serological results, WNV was diagnosed in 63 of the 129 horses presenting neurological signs. These findings reinforce the continued circulation of WNV in Portugal and highlight the importance of sustained surveillance in equine populations.

title: Inter- and intra-rater reliability of two grading systems for equine gastric glandular disease.
abstract: The recommended combined descriptive terminology scoring system for equine gastric glandular disease has poor reliability whereas a published numerical scoring system has substantial reliability. Descriptive terminology appears more affected by clinical experience than numerical scoring. Individual descriptive terminologies have previously correlated with descriptions of severity. To compare the reliability of two scoring systems across varied clinical experience and between numerical scores and descriptive terms. The hypothesis was that the numerical scoring system would have better reliability regardless of clinical experience and numerical scores would correlate with individual descriptive terms. Prospective, blinded observer study. Duplicate gastroscopy images of 30 glandular lesions were assessed by 12 raters using both scoring systems; raters were split into four groups: internal medicine specialists, residents, general practitioners and new graduates. Intra- and inter-rater reliability of both systems and individual criteria therein were determined using Krippendorff's alpha. Intra and inter-rater reliability were higher for the numerical scoring system when assessing all raters combined (α = 0.89, 95% CI 0.86-0.90 and α = 0.67, 95% CI 0.65-0.69 respectively) compared to the combined descriptive terminology system (α = 0.61, 95% CI 0.55-0.66 and α = 0.09, 95% CI 0.08-0.10 respectively). Intra-rater reliability was high for all groups with the numerical system, but only high for specialists with the descriptive system. Intra-rater reliability was more affected in the descriptive scoring system by clinical experience than the numerical scoring system. Inter-rater reliability was moderate for specialists, residents and recent graduates with the numerical system, but poor for all groups with the descriptive system. There was a large and statistically significant association between numerical score and the score for 'severity' (η2_H = 0.66, 95% CI 0.52-0.75; p < 0.001). Use of still images visualised on individual screens. The numerical scoring system was more reliable than the descriptive system regardless of clinical experience. Numerical score and 'severity' are strongly associated.

title: Feed protein partitioning impacts horse fecal nitrogen profiles: A retrospective pilot study.
abstract: Feeding horses excess crude protein (CP) leads to increased nitrogen excretion in urine and feces. However, evidence is lacking in how CP partitioning in the diet impacts nitrogen profiles in equine feces for potential fertilizer use. Thus, our retrospective pilot study objective was to determine if daily CP and neutral detergent soluble CP (NDSCP) intakes affected equine fecal nitrogen profiles. Three Quarter Horse geldings were fed 15 g dry matter (DM)/kg body weight (BW)/d of coastal Bermudagrass hay for 14 d (GRASS) then 15 g DM/kg BW/d of a 50:50 mixture of coastal Bermudagrass and alfalfa hay for 14 d (MIXED). A concentrate with 158 g CP/kg DM was fed daily (0.5 kg DM/d). Fresh feces were collected on Day 14 of each phase and frozen at -80°C, then analyzed by Dairy One (Ithaca, NY, USA). Intake data (g/kg BW/d) and fecal analyses (g/kg DM) were analyzed using a paired t-test and ANCOVA using CP intake as a covariate. The MIXED diet provided more NDSCP (2.04 g NDSCP/kg BW/d) than GRASS (1.50 g NDSCP/kg BW/d; P < 0.001). Fecal ammonia concentration tended greater and fecal carbon concentration was less in MIXED versus GRASS (P = 0.082; P = 0.015). From the ANCOVA, MIXED had greater fecal ammonia (P = 0.047) but less fecal-N (P = 0.018) and organic-N (P = 0.007) than GRASS. Increases in dietary NDSCP from greater CP intake increase excretion of nitrogen as fecal ammonia in a single hand-grab sample, which indicates that dietary protein fractionation may impact equine fecal nitrogen profiles and therefore, manure management.

title: Metabolite changes in equine amniotic fluid associated with experimentally induced ascending placentitis.
abstract: Equine ascending placentitis is a major cause of late-term pregnancy loss and stillbirth. However, early diagnosis remains limited, and its effect on amniotic fluid metabolite composition is poorly understood. Characterize alterations in the amniotic fluid metabolome of mares with experimentally induced ascending placentitis. This was a controlled experimental study. At 280 days of gestation, six pony mares received an intracervical inoculation of Streptococcus equi subspecies zooepidemicus (placentitis group), and five mares were left untreated (control group). Placentitis mares developed signs of placental inflammation and were euthanized 8 days post-inoculation. Control mares were euthanized at corresponding gestational ages. Amniotic fluid was collected immediately after euthanasia and analyzed by untargeted liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry. Metabolites were annotated against a spectral library, with a match score above 60% considered a confident identification. Eighteen metabolites differed between groups (P ≤ 0.05). Two were confidently identified. L-threonine was lower in placentitis mares than in control mares. L-isoleucine was higher in placentitis mares than in control mares. In mares with ascending placentitis induced at 280 days of gestation, the amniotic fluid metabolome was altered, including decreased L-threonine and increased L-isoleucine.

title: A scoping review of equine musculoskeletal therapy interventions to inform evidence-based decision making.
abstract: Equine musculoskeletal therapy interventions are increasingly used in management and rehabilitation of musculoskeletal disorders. Consolidation of the evidence base would facilitate collaboration between veterinarians and veterinary physiotherapists. This scoping review aimed to identify, categorise, and summarise the current evidence on equine musculoskeletal therapy interventions. The study followed the Joanna Briggs Institute methodology for a scoping review. CAB Abstracts, Web of Science, and PubMed databases were searched and reviewed against inclusion criteria. Publications evaluating hydrotherapy, massage, stretching, myofascial release, osteopathy, chiropractic interventions, TENS, therapeutic ultrasound, kinesiotherapy, trigger point release, reflex inhibition, and thermotherapy for equids were included and reviewed. Data were extracted and charted according to study aim, study design, musculoskeletal therapy intervention, population, assessment methods, and outcome. 2,340 publications were identified; following duplicate removal, 1,874 were screened and 74 met inclusion criteria. Thirteen intervention categories were identified. Massage, chiropractic interventions, dynamic mobilisation and hydrotherapy were the most frequently studied, with 11-14 publications each. There were between 1-6 studies for each of the other interventions. There were considerable variations in intervention delivery, study design, and outcome assessment which limited ability to consolidate evidence. The greatest body and consistency of evidence was for dynamic mobilisation and massage. This is the largest published evidence review of equine musculoskeletal therapy interventions to date, encompassing 13 categories. Variation in study design and outcomes limited comparison and the ability to generate evidence-based recommendations. Standardised terminology, consistent study design and reporting will strengthen the evidence base and aid clinical integration.

title: Effect of canagliflozin on insulin sensitivity in insulin-dysregulated horses as assessed by euglycemic hyperinsulinemic clamp: a randomized, placebo-controlled trial.
abstract: Insulin resistance, enhanced β-cell responsiveness, and lower insulin clearance contribute to hyperinsulinemia in horses with insulin dysregulation. Canagliflozin (CAN) reduces hyperinsulinemia in horses, but its effect on insulin sensitivity (IS) remains unclear. Evaluate the effects of CAN on IS and insulin clearance using a euglycemic hyperinsulinemic clamp (EHC) and on β-cell responsiveness using a graded glucose infusion test (GGI) in insulin-dysregulated (ID) horses. Twenty privately owned ID mares. In this randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study, horses received CAN (0.4 mg/kg, n = 10) or placebo (PBO, n = 10) PO once daily for 4 weeks. Insulin sensitivity and insulin metabolic clearance rate (MCR) were assessed by EHC, and β-cell responsiveness by GGI. Insulin sensitivity (M/I) was lower with CAN than PBO (1.5 ± 0.2 vs 2.7 ± 0.2 [mg/kg/min × 103]/[μIU/mL]; LS mean difference,-1.3 [95% CI, -1.9 to -0.6]; P < .001), whereas insulin MCR was higher (6.5 ± 0.3 vs 5.4 ± 0.3 mL/kg/min; LS mean difference, 1.0 [95% CI, 0.3-1.8]; P = .01). Beta-cell responsiveness (ΔI vs ΔG) was 43.3% lower with CAN (20.8 [95% CI, 16.9-25.5] vs 36.7 [29.9-45.1] mIU/mmol; ratio of geometric LS means, 0.57 [95% CI, 0.42-0.76]; P < .001). Beta-cell responsiveness was lower and insulin clearance higher in CAN-treated ID mares, despite apparently lower IS. Higher endogenous glucose production in CAN-treated mares might have contributed to an underestimation of IS.

title: Equine herpesvirus 1 myeloencephalopathy incidence and case fatality rates in the USA.
abstract: Equine herpesvirus 1 (EHV-1) myeloencephalopathy (EHM) has substantial animal welfare and economic consequences. Despite extensive research, population-level estimates of EHM incidence and case fatality rates remain poorly characterized. Describe the burden of EHM and estimate EHM attack and case fatality rates in the United States. None. A retrospective observational study was conducted using surveillance data collected by the Equine Disease Communication Center (EDCC) in the United States during 2019-2023. Regression models were used to estimate the mean annual EHM incidence and to quantify attack and fatality rates. The incidence and potential seasonality of EHM by age category were also assessed. Surveillance data showed that isolated EHM cases predominated, and the estimated mean annual incidence in the United States was 6.7 per million horses (95% CI, 4.9-8.9). The attack rate was 4.3% (95% CI, 3.5-5.4) and the case fatality rate was 49.5% (95% CI, 40.5-60.5). In the United States, older horses (>19 years) had higher EHM incidence than younger horses. Cases were more frequent from January to June, peaking in March. Equine herpesvirus 1 myeloencephalopathy is an uncommon clinical manifestation of EHV-1 infection, but the high case fatality rate emphasizes the clinical relevance of this condition.

title: Identification of a novel equine rotavirus B from Missouri in 2025, which is distantly related to group B rotaviruses.
abstract: Despite the wide circulation of group B rotaviruses in animals and humans, rotavirus B was not found in horses until 2021 in Kentucky, USA. Little is known about the genetic diversity and evolution of rotavirus B in this new host. Here, we described a divergent equine rotavirus B (ERVB) from a foal with idiopathic diarrhea in Missouri (designated MO-ERVB-25). Full-genome sequencing and phylogenetic analysis revealed that MO-ERVB-25 is distantly related to all previously known group B rotaviruses, including ERVB strains identified in 2021 in Kentucky (KY-ERVB-21). The mean nucleotide substitution rate of the VP4 segment was estimated as 1.44 × 10-3 substitutions/site/year, which is a magnitude higher than the VP7 segment. We further demonstrated that MO-ERVB-25, like human RVB, binds chemically neutral LacNAc-containing complex N-linked glycans, while KY-ERVB-21 recognizes negatively charged polysialic acid (polySia) with α-2,8-linkage, which is a functional receptor for unrelated enteric human adenovirus 52. Using the AlphaFold-enabled structure prediction, we showed that both MO-ERVB-25 and human RVB VP8* lack a novel C-terminal α2 helix that is only observed in the KY-ERVB-21 VP8*, which may help explain the difference in glycan binding specificities. Finally, screening of foal samples by the reverse transcription quantitative PCR assay identified 4.2% of idiopathic foal diarrhea samples (6 out of 140) positive for MO-ERVB-25. These results suggest that MO-ERVB-25 represents a new rotavirus B subgroup that circulates in foals. Its circulation, together with KY-ERVB-25 subgroup, raises the possibility of reassortment and antigenic shift as mechanisms of rotavirus B evolution in equines. Equine RVB (ERVB) has emerged as a significant cause of foal diarrhea since 2021. Our study describes a highly divergent RVB strain identified in a foal with severe diarrhea in 2025. This ERVB variant exhibited low amino acid identity compared with previously reported ERVB strains. The novel ERVB strain escaped routine diagnostic detection. Sequence analysis demonstrated that this new strain grouped with bovine, porcine, caprine, and equine RVB but formed a distinct, independent branch. In addition, glycan array studies revealed the substantial difference in glycan recognition between new and previously described ERVB strains, which is likely determined by the presence or absence of a novel C-terminal α2 helix in the VP8* receptor-binding domain. These results suggest that this novel ERVB variant may co-circulate with existing ERVB strains in horses, which may facilitate rapid viral evolution through antigenic diversity, a property previously reported in rotaviruses from other hosts.

title: Effectiveness of Hippotherapy in Balance Rehabilitation for Stroke Patients: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.
abstract: Stroke frequently leads to balance and mobility impairments, significantly affecting patients' independence and quality of life. Hippotherapy, a therapy involving horse-based movements, has gained attention as a potential intervention for balance rehabilitation. This study evaluates the effectiveness of hippotherapy in improving balance and mobility in stroke patients. A systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted following PRISMA guidelines through PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, Embase, Cochrane Library, and Physiotherapy Evidence Database for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) assessing hippotherapy's effects on balance in adult stroke patients (Prospero registration number: CRD42024552688). Effect sizes were pooled using RevMan software. Ten RCTs met the inclusion criteria, with seven included in the meta-analysis (n = 389 participants). Hippotherapy significantly improved balance outcomes compared to conventional exercise programs, as measured by the Berg Balance Scale (BBS) (mean difference [MD] =1.72; 95% confidence interval [CI] [1.38, 2.07], P < 0.00001) and the timed up and go (TUG) test (MD = -2.97 s; 95% CI [-4.83, -1.11], P = 0.002). Exploratory subgroup analysis showed no statistically significant difference between mechanical and real-horse hippotherapy (P = 0.64). Stroke patients may benefit from hippotherapy as an effective adjunct to conventional rehabilitation. Hippotherapy significantly improves balance and functional mobility, as demonstrated by improvements in the BBS and TUG test. However, evidence regarding quality of life and psychological outcomes remains limited and inconclusive, underscoring the need for further high-quality RCTs.

title: The Tango of cGAS-STING and Phagocytosis in Disease: From Molecular Mechanisms to Pharmacological Targeting.
abstract: The cGAS-STING pathway is a central cytosolic DNA sensor that orchestrates innate immune responses beyond type I interferons, including autophagy, senescence, metabolism, and cell death. Phagocytosis-essential for clearing pathogens, debris, and apoptotic bodies-critically bridges innate and adaptive immunity. This review examines the bidirectional, context-dependent interplay between these fundamental processes and highlights how nanotechnology is uniquely positioned to exploit this crosstalk for therapeutic gain. We delineate four paradigms: STING activation upstream induces phagocytosis in lung inflammation, sepsis, spinal cord injury, cancer, and viral infection; phagocytosis initiates STING by delivering immunogenic cargo; positive feedback loops amplify antitumor immunity; and STING can suppress phagocytosis in obesity-driven adipose inflammation. Importantly, this axis exerts opposing regulatory effects across disease settings, being protective or pathogenic, synergistic or antagonistic, depending on cell type, stimulus, and pathological context. We further synthesize advanced nanoplatforms-biomimetic nanoparticles, hybrid membrane vesicles, DNA nanodevices, lymph node-targeted nanovaccines, and "Trojan horse" nanocapsules-engineered to co-deliver STING agonists, phagocytosis checkpoint inhibitors, and immunogenic cargo. These nanotherapies enhance antitumor and antimicrobial defense, resolve inflammation, and overcome barriers such as the blood-brain barrier. By integrating mechanism with nanobiotechnology, this review provides a conceptual framework for the cGAS -STING-phagocytosis network and a roadmap for next-generation nanomedicines treating cancer, infection, neurodegeneration, and inflammatory disorders.

title: Periprosthetic Joint Infection Caused by Streptococcus equi Subspecies zooepidemicus: The First Reported Case Confirmed by Synovial Fluid Culture.
abstract: Streptococcus equi subspecies zooepidemicus (SEZ) is a pathogen associated with infections in horses. It can occasionally transmit and cause clinical infections in humans. Even though the bacterium is an opportunistic pathogen, human infections are often severe such as meningitis, septicemia, endocarditis, and septic arthritis. We report a unique case of synovial fluid culture-confirmed periprosthetic joint infection (PJI) caused by SEZ. The patient had undergone a total knee arthroplasty due to osteoarthritis. Five months postoperatively, she was admitted to the hospital with fever and clinical signs of PJI of the knee. The bacterial culture of the synovial fluid and blood cultures revealed SEZ. The 16S rRNA polymerase chain reaction (16S rRNA PCR) and culture of perioperative synovial tissue samples confirmed the same bacterium. Within 48 h of the onset of PJI symptoms, an operation with DAIR (debridement, antibiotics, and implant retention) was performed and followed by 12 weeks of antibiotic therapy. The prosthetic joint was preserved, and the patient had fully recovered with no signs of infection relapse at the 2-year follow-up. Two weeks prior to the PJI symptoms, the patient had visited a horse stable, where one of the horses had symptoms of an upper respiratory infection. We present the first case of synovial fluid culture-confirmed PJI caused by SEZ described in the literature. SEZ can be transmitted from horses to humans and cause serious infections, including PJI. The bacterium should be kept in mind when investigating acute infections, including PJI, in people who encounter horses due to their profession or hobbies.

title: Humoral immune responses and adverse effects of inactivated West Nile virus and tetanus toxoid vaccines administered via the subcutaneous or intramuscular route in horses.
abstract: Myosin heavy chain myopathy (MYHM) is a genetic disorder in Quarter Horse-related breeds that can result in non-exertional rhabdomyolysis and immune-mediated myositis. Infectious diseases and muscle damage, particularly from intramuscular (IM) vaccination, have been implicated as potential triggers for this condition. However, the subcutaneous (SC) injection route has not been investigated as an alternative vaccination method for MYHM-affected horses. The hypothesis was that there would be no difference in humoral immune responses or injection site reactions in healthy horses receiving killed West Nile virus (WNV) and tetanus toxoid vaccines via SC and IM routes. The primary objective was to determine serum antibody titers and the adverse effects elicited by both vaccination routes. A randomized, single-blind, two-arm, two-period study compared the responses in horses receiving WNV and tetanus vaccines via IM or SC routes. A total of 17 adult mares, all of which were negative for the MYH1 mutation, from a university research and teaching herd were included in the study. Serum antibody levels were assessed on the day of each vaccination. Antibody levels were also assessed on days 28 and 56 after WNV vaccine and on day 28 after tetanus toxoid administration. Vaccine site reactions were assessed daily for 72 h after vaccination. Antibody levels and injection site reactions were analyzed using two-way repeated measures ANOVA, rank sum tests, and Fisher's exact test, with statistical significance at a p-value of <0.05. Serum neutralization antibody titers increased after WNV vaccination regardless of the route of vaccine administration (p = 0.007), with no differences observed between routes of administration. Injection site swelling was greater after SC vaccination than after IM injection route for the WNV vaccine (p = 0.003). Baseline tetanus titers were high in almost all horses, and no change in titer was observed following vaccination. Injection site swelling was greater after SC tetanus vaccination than after IM vaccination (p = 0.002). Subcutaneous vaccination was associated with significant local reactions. An accurate assessment of humoral responses was challenging as the horses included in the study had high baseline titers from previous vaccinations. As a result, drawing definitive conclusions regarding the equivalence of responses to SC versus IM vaccination is difficult. Therefore, the results regarding this comparison must be considered inconclusive.

title: Sustainability stories in Swedish riding schools: an ecolinguistic analysis of policy documents and interviews.
journal: Frontiers in sports and active living
abstract: The equine sector provides employment opportunities and leisure activities for a substantial number of people in Sweden. Although these activities are closely connected to nature and dependent on ecosystem services, the sector faces significant ecological challenges. This article explores how representatives of the equine sector-particularly riding schools-conceptualize and articulate their work with environmental sustainability in policy documents and "talk about" everyday practice. The analysis is informed by the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and grounded in an ecolinguistic framework. Our results show that national level policy documents are closely aligned with the established sustainability terminology, whereas local documents and interviewees rarely employ SDG related terminology. Despite this discursive distance, riding schools demonstrate strong engagement and considerable creativity in addressing local environmental challenges. However, this ambition is constrained by limited knowledge, resources, and authority to address more complex ecological issues. Within the pedagogical environments that riding schools constitute, systematic instruction on environmental sustainability holds a marginal position. We identified five "stories we live by": "the responsible local care taker", "we try, but we lack resources", "learning through everyday practice", "sustainability without sustainability terminology" and "small action matters". We have interpreted this as emerging eco-benifical narratives that can carry pedagogical potential. We argue that with strengthened organizational support, clearer conceptual tools, and structured opportunities for capacity building, riding schools could play a more active role in shaping sustainability-oriented "stories to live by" and contribute more fully to the broader societal transition toward sustainable development.

title: Comparative study of in vitro digestibility and antioxidant activities of whey from different milks.
abstract: Whey proteins, a protein-rich by-product of milk, contribute to various biological benefits. These bioactivities play an important role in human health and can be enhanced when whey proteins are digested, yet the digestion of whey proteins from different animal species under standardized protocols of in vitro digestion and its effect on antioxidant activity remain insufficiently characterized. This work aims to compare the digestibility and antioxidant activities of whey from the milk of different animal species: cameline, bovine, ovine, caprine, and equine. Milk samples from the five species were coagulated to obtain whey. The whey proteins were digested with pepsin and pancreatin in an in vitro process that mimics digestion in the gastrointestinal tract. Physicochemical parameters, protein profiles (SDS‑PAGE), peptide concentration, degree of hydrolysis (DH), and antioxidant activities were analyzed to assess inter‑species differences. After milk coagulation, a slight increase in pH values was observed in all whey samples. The maximum peptide concentration was observed in the digested ewe whey, while digested mare whey showed the lowest. Camel whey has the highest content of sodium, potassium, zinc and iron, while goat whey has the highest concentration of copper and ewe whey has the highest concentration of calcium. The SDS-PAGE profiles showed that all five milk types had an identical protein profile, with the exception of camel whey, which was characterised by the absence of β-lactoglobulin (β-Lg) and the presence of two different proteins camel whey basic protein (CWBP) and Peptidoglycan recognition protein (PGRP). The highest antioxidant activity was found in ewe whey. The sensitivity of whey proteins to hydrolysis varies between milk types. Correlation analysis indicated that the DH was significantly positively correlated with peptide concentrations (r = 0.998, p < 0.0001), indicating that increased proteolysis facilitates peptide liberation. Simulated gastrointestinal digestion produced peptides exhibiting antioxidant properties across all five species, reinforcing the notion that whey hydrolysates offer a valuable avenue for enhancing this by-product. These findings highlight the nutritional and functional diversity of whey proteins among animal species. Hydrolysates of whey proteins from all animal species studied could be an interesting approach to add value to this by-product.

title: Anatomical and computed tomographic study of equine cervical spinal nerves and intervertebral foramina.
abstract: Osseous enlargement of the cervical articular process joints due to osteoarthropathy or developmental hypertrophy can narrow the intervertebral foramen (IF), resulting in compression and neuritis of the exiting spinal nerves. Associated clinical signs may include neck pain, forelimb lameness or muscle atrophy. Computed tomography (CT) is the gold standard for IF evaluation; however, to date, visualisation of the equine spinal nerves based on CT imaging is insufficient. To improve the diagnostic accuracy of foraminal stenosis and cervical spinal nerve (CSN) compression based on CT, this study aims to describe the anatomical size and position of the CSN at the level of the IF. Cadaveric study. Anatomical dissection was performed to expose the dorsal and ventral rami of CSN3-CSN8 in 10 cervical specimens (n = 88 IF and CSN). Barium sulfate was applied to the nerves, and CT imaging was performed. The cross-sectional area (CSA) of the IF and CSN, the CSN shape and position within the foramen were quantified. Both IF and CSN CSA significantly increased caudally, with the largest values identified at C7-Th1. The ratio of the spinal nerves CSA to IF CSA was significantly higher caudally, suggesting a greater risk of compression in this region. The CSN position within the IF varied between vertebral levels and was positioned in the mid-caudal third of the IF between C3 and C6 and more cranial in the IFs between C6 and Th1. Ex vivo character of the study and the relatively small sample size. These findings demonstrate significant anatomical variation in the size, shape and position of the CSN inside the IF depending on the vertebral level. Detailed knowledge of these patterns enables increased diagnostic precision and the development of targeted therapeutic interventions in equine CSN compression.

title: A Subclinical Biomechanical Phenotype Detected By AI-Assisted Video Gait Analysis in Horses Heterozygous for the Fragile Foal Syndrome Allele in PLOD1.
abstract: The domestic horse has unmatched within-species polymorphism in locomotor patterns and provides an advantageous model of genetic influence on locomotion. Fragile Foal Syndrome (FFS) results from a missense mutation in the Procollagen-lysine,2-oxoglutarate 5-dioxygenase 1 (PLOD1), resulting in reduced collagen crosslinking with potential biomechanical consequences. To further understand the effect of the carrier genotype on locomotor phenotypes, we examined kinematic variation using a matched case-control design within a large sport horse cohort genotyped for the FFS variant. We characterized eight kinematic parameters derived from AI-assisted video analysis across a cohort of 128 sport horses. Carrier frequency was compared to previously published references using Fisher's exact test. We tested the relationship between locomotor phenotypes and the FFS genotype with a matched subset of 20 horses (8 carriers, 12 wildtype), analyzed using Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) regression blocking by facility and applying a BH-FDR correction. Warmbloods trotted faster than Thoroughbreds (P_BH = 0.020). The FFS carrier frequency among Thoroughbreds in this population (7.02%) was significantly higher than previously reported (1.4%, P = 0.010). Within the matched cohort, FFS carriers demonstrated significantly higher duty factor (P_BH = 0.021) and tended to have a greater hindlimb retraction ratio (P_raw = 0.013, P_BH = 0.051). Although limited by a small sample and a pilot analysis pipeline focused on the right hindlimb, we observed changes in gait consistent with increased connective tissue compliance among FFS carriers. AI-assisted digital kinematics provides a feasible approach for high-throughput evaluation of locomotor phenotypes in the horse.

title: Transrectal ultrasonographic assessment of the equine fetal distal limb beyond the first phalanx for predicting fetal age and bone development in Quarter Horses.
abstract: In Quarter Horses (QH), fetal age can be predicted within 2 weeks prior to 200- days of gestation ultrasonographically; however, as pregnancy advances, accuracy decreases. Recently, fetal ultrasonographic measurement of the first phalanx length (P1L) was introduced as a novel biometric parameter during late gestation, and the timing of appearance and closure of P1 epiphyses has been identified as potential markers of bone development. The overall aim of this study is to describe distal limb bone development beyond the first phalanx. Ten healthy pregnant mares (9 QH and 1 Thoroughbred carrying a QH fetus) with known ovulation dates were used. Transrectal ultrasonography was performed every 2 weeks from 9 months of gestation until parturition. P2 length (P2L) correlated highly with days of gestation (p < 0.0001; r2 = 0.75). A correlation equation was established: y = 5.343 (±0.403) x +205.1(±6.99) (y = predicted value of gestational age in days; x = P2 length in mm).
